analysis.one_liner: Bans stock trading by Members of Congress, the President, justices, and Fed officials.
analysis.headline: Solely sponsored in December 2023 with no cosponsors, the bill sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop senior government officials from personally buying and selling stocks, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency, and would force them to sell any such holdings within about four months of taking office. Members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and top Federal Reserve officials would be covered, along with their spouses and dependent children. It would also require officials to disclose when they or their families seek or receive federal money such as contracts, grants, or loans, and would make all financial disclosures searchable online, including for federal judges.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to know that the people writing laws, setting monetary policy, and deciding cases are not simultaneously betting on the companies those decisions affect. The public gains searchable, sortable online databases of every official's finances, and new disclosure whenever an official or their family applies for or receives a federal payment.

how_it_helps.text: Bars covered officials and their spouses and dependent children from holding, buying, or selling securities, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency, including through synthetic positions like options and derivatives [S2].

Requires divestiture of existing holdings within 120 days, with a fine of at least 10 percent of the value of any interest held or traded in violation, and makes the ban apply even to holdings in trusts where the official is a beneficial owner, regardless of whether the trust is a qualified blind trust [S2].

Requires senior officials to report, within 30 to 45 days, any application for or receipt of a covered federal payment — including loans, contracts, and grants — by themselves, their spouse, or a dependent child, with a $5,000 fine for failing to report [S2].
Extends financial disclosure and transaction-reporting rules to presidents, vice presidents, and directors of Federal Reserve banks, officials not currently covered [S2].

Requires electronic filing and public, searchable databases of disclosure reports for Members of Congress, senior executive branch officials, judicial officers, and Federal Reserve bank officers, with data sortable by filer name, asset, ticker symbol, and transaction date and accessible through an API [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve officials, and their families, who would have to sell individual stock holdings, forgo active securities trading during their service, and file detailed disclosure reports. Financial services firms would lose the small share of trading activity that comes from these officials.

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the existing criminal fine provision for failing to file a transaction report with a flat $1,000 civil fine, a penalty that may be easier to absorb as a cost of doing business for wealthy officials [S2].

Enforcement of the trading ban relies on supervising ethics offices assessing fines rather than on prosecutors or courts, so compliance depends on bodies with a mixed record of policing their own [S2].

The bill exempts diversified mutual funds, Treasury securities, and a spouse's compensation or stock from their primary employer, so officials could retain substantial market exposure and, in the case of a spouse's employer stock, potentially keep shares in a company their household's other breadwinner works for [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: officials give up the ability to trade individual securities and spouses lose some flexibility, in exchange for removing the appearance and reality of officials profiting from their own decisions. The narrow exemptions are the standard accommodations used in similar proposals and do not swallow the rule, but the all-civil enforcement scheme and the downgraded $1,000 fine for late transaction reports are weaknesses an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no further action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, so the bill died without a hearing, markup, or vote [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the bill on December 18, 2023, near the end of the first session of the 118th Congress [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, the standard first step for such bills [S4].
No cosponsors joined from either party during the bill's lifetime [S3].

The bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and its committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in its action history before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders. Because the bill never advanced, Members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and Federal Reserve officials kept their existing right to trade individual stocks, and the disclosure gaps the bill targeted — including Federal Reserve bank officials and blind trusts — remain as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent officials who kept their trading rights

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 3555 on December 18, 2023; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (Chair: Sen. Gary Peters, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the 118th Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote; its action history shows nothing after the December 18, 2023 referral.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Senate party leaders of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor action on S. 3555 or any competing congressional stock-trading ban during the 118th Congress, despite multiple similar bills and sustained public pressure on the issue.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator besides the sponsor signed on, from either party, so the bill never revealed a partisan split [S3].

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders (Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve officials)
industries.note: These officials are the regulated class here: the bill would bar them and their families from trading individual stocks and force divestiture of existing holdings. Their interest in keeping the status quo ran directly against the transparency the bill promised the public. The bill died, so their existing rights remain untouched.

Firms would lose the modest trading volume from a few hundred senior officials and their families, and would face a searchable public database of officials' transactions. The effect on the industry overall is small, which is part of why industry opposition was never the central fight here.

Federal Reserve bank presidents, vice presidents, and directors would newly be subject to financial disclosure and trading rules, with the Board's Inspector General as their ethics office. Several Fed officials resigned in 2020 after trading disclosures, making this a targeted fix for a known gap.
